survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA public-use microdata for Austria and Scotland from 2012, 2015, and 2018, focusing on 15-year-olds (age window 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) sampled via a two-stage design (schools stratified, then students randomly selected within schools). All statistical inference is stated to account for the complex sample design using resampling methods with replicate weights provided in the PISA databases, implemented via the Stata package repest. The paper also relies on PISA’s multiply imputed test scores (plausible values) rather than single test scores, and includes covariates (gender, immigrant background, and socio-economic status quartiles) in the main difference-in-differences regressions. The manuscript does not explicitly name a specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it does explicitly state that inference accounts for the sampling design through replicate weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2012, 2015, and 2018 data for Austria and Scotland only. The analytic strategy exploits that these jurisdictions changed PISA testing dates across cycles (Austria: early-testing years 2012 and 2018; late-testing year 2015; Scotland: early-testing years 2012 and 2015; late-testing year 2018). The identification compares students grouped by month of birth within the PISA 12-month eligibility window, contrasting months whose expected age/grade differ in late- vs early-testing years, and estimates grade-and-age effects via a difference-in-differences specification with year fixed effects and month-of-birth dummies. Robustness checks include placebo difference-in-differences restricted to years with unchanged testing dates, a made-up subgroup comparison within early-testing years, and a leave-one-out estimator excluding one month of birth at a time.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper estimates learning gains over one school year for 15-year-olds in Austria and Scotland by combining multiple PISA cycles (2012, 2015, 2018) and exploiting changes in PISA testing dates across cycles. The dependent variables are PISA reading, mathematics, and science scores derived from item-response theory and analyzed using multiply imputed plausible values (PISA PVs). The core identification uses a difference-in-differences design comparing students grouped by month of birth across early- vs late-testing years, with year fixed effects and month-of-birth dummies; covariates include gender, immigrant background, and socio-economic status quartiles. The estimated grade-and-age effects are about one-fourth of a standard deviation (≈25 score points) in each subject, with robustness checks including parallel-trends placebos and leave-one-out by month of birth. Limitations include reliance on the common-trend assumption and the fact that PISA was not designed specifically to measure grade-and-age effects, leading to relatively large statistical uncertainty for subgroup comparisons.
